content: The WHO Steering Group was responsible for providing high-level oversight throughout the development of the guidelines. This group included members from WHO headquarters in Geneva, six regional offices, and two country offices. Key contributors included Alarcos Cieza, focusing on disability and rehabilitation at WHO headquarters, and Ameer Mohammad, addressing disability, injury, assistive technology, and rehabilitation in the South-East Asia Regional Office. Other notable contributors were Antony Duttine from the Americas Regional Office, Bianca Hemmingsen from Geneva focusing on noncommunicable diseases, and Edith Andrews Annan from the Africa Regional Office specializing in medicines and health products. The Guidelines Development Group (GDG) played a critical role in shaping the scope of the guidelines. They developed key questions in the PICO format, selected and rated outcomes to guide evidence reviews, interpreted evidence with explicit consideration of the balance of benefits and harms, and contributed to content development. The group also reviewed and approved the final guidelines. Membership was diverse, representing various ages, genders, settings, and experiences in accessing health and wheelchair services, as well as policy development. The External Review Group (ERG) provided feedback to identify errors, missing data, and context-specific issues. They also commented on the clarity and implications of the guidelines for implementation. Members included individuals who might use or implement the guidelines, as well as those impacted by them. The systematic review team was commissioned to inform the guidelines. This team, selected through WHO’s procurement processes, ensured expertise in evidence assessment using the GRADE approach. They had no financial conflicts of interest. The WHO Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics (CRE) policy was followed to manage conflicts of interest. Members of the GDG, ERG, external partners, observers, authors, and methodologists completed the WHO Declaration of Interests (DOI) form. These forms were reviewed individually by the WHO Secretariat to assess whether any declared interests represented a conflict that could affect judgment during evidence assessment or recommendation formulation. No declarations were found to represent conflicts of interest that would preclude participation. Several contributors declared interests related to their professional roles. For example, David Constantine held an office representing interests related to the subject of the meeting. Emma Smith conducted consultancies and received research funding in related areas. Lamia Al Faleh managed rehabilitation services, including wheelchair provision. Silvana Contepomi provided consultancy and advisory services to organizations involved in wheelchair provision. Mary Goldberg and Jon Pearlman were employed in academic institutions and engaged in related research, with Pearlman also being a co-inventor of wheelchairs with patents owned by his employer. Other contributors, such as Eric Wunderlich and Ferdiliza Dandah Garcia, provided consultancy services and represented stakeholder groups in leadership and advocacy roles. Jamie Noon offered consultancy services to various organizations on wheelchair provision and training. Koly Kamrunnaher supported research for academic institutions, while Laura Cohen consulted for national bodies and conducted research funded by grants. Rory Cooper applied for patents for wheelchairs, and Rosemary Joan Gowran acted as a consultant and advisor for international wheelchair provision projects. External partners and observers, including representatives from organizations like the International Society of Wheelchair Professionals and UNICEF, participated in technical meetings and provided input during the development process.
